title: Adaptive echo-batcher: attention skim, admission scoring, and straggler redemption
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: Implement an adaptive admission/batching component ("echo-batcher") that computes a lightweight admission score per request to decide: immediate admission, short-hold for a shaping window, or speculative prefetch of KV/attention state. The admission score ("echo score") captures prefix reuse likelihood, estimated attention locality, and kernel-fit probability to optimize kernel selection and prefill scheduling.

Motivation: Current continuous batching sacrifices tail-latency SLAs under mixed-request loads (short chat turns + long generation bursts). We need a low-overhead classifier that: reduces harmful microbursts to the GPU, enables kernel affinity decisions earlier, and drives attention-prefetch heuristics to reduce decode-time stalls. Traditional quantile gating alone is brittle for heterogeneous customers; echo-batcher should generalize across models and sequence distributions.

Design overview:
- Echo score generation: a compact feature vector computed at ingress including: prefix_length, recent-token-entropy-estimate, model_variant_hint, cached-kv-hit-estimate, and historical-kernel-latency-mean (from per-route telemetry). Score is produced by a small ensemble (rule-smoother + logistic regressor) that runs in the admission path.
- Admission policy: three outcomes — admit-now, short-buffer(10-40ms) for shaping, speculative-prefetch. Short-buffer windows are dynamically sized by current GPU load and predicted decode cost. Speculative-prefetch triggers an async KV warm path + early attention-skim.
- Attention skim: during speculative-prefetch we run a fast reduced-precision attention pass (skimming top-k tokens by token-similarity heuristics) to surface hotspots and hint the kernel selector whether to prefer dense vs block-sparse kernels for the upcoming decode. This is gated to keep CPU/GPU overhead small (<5% of a request).
- Straggler redemption: requests predicted to be stragglers are given a small priority credit and routed to a fallback kernel path (lower memory but higher latency) to avoid head-of-line blocking for other batches. Credits decay over time to prevent starvation.

Implementation plan:
Phase 0 (sim + feature engineering): build offline simulator using recent traffic traces; evaluate echo score correlation with p95/p99.
Phase 1 (admission service): lightweight Go service integrated into edge gateway; expose scoring API and admission policy config.
Phase 2 (runtime integration): runtime hooks for speculative-prefetch, attention skim calls, and kernel affinity hints. Add metrics and tracing spans.
Phase 3 (gradual rollout): canary on low-traffic routes, A/B with circuit-breaker to revert if cost/regression observed.

Success metrics (initial targets):
- p99 tail-latency reduction: >= 15% on mixed workloads
- p95 latency: <= 5% regression
- overall throughput: >= 5% uplift due to better packing
- decode stalls reduced by >= 30% (measured by blocked-decode time)
- additional compute overhead: <= 3% cost increase for speculative ops (configurable)

Trade-offs and risks:
- Speculative prefetch increases work and possibly cost; we mitigate via tight gating and rollout quotas.
- Attention skim correctness: false positives (skimming wrong tokens) could mislead kernel selection; keep kernel fallbacks available.
- Model drift: echo score model must be periodically retrained; plan to backfill nightly jobs to refresh weights.

Open questions:
- What telemetry window is best for historical-kernel-latency (30s vs 5min)?
- What safe default short-buffer window minimizes both p99 and throughput loss?
- Do we expose fine-grained controls to customers (per-route admission policy)?

Operational notes:
- Add new tracing tags: admission.echo_score, admission.outcome, skim.tokens, kernel.hint.
- Rollout guard: global kill switch + per-customer budget.
- Backward compatibility: when admission service is unreachable, fall back to admit-now behavior.

Artifacts: design doc (drive link): https://drive.google.com/drive/fake-link/echo-batcher-design, initial simulator results in notebook: https://gist.github.com/redwood/echo-sim-2026, corresponding runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/8123.
